svg.title: The world model
svg.desc: Every host has a memory of 100 numbers. Events arrive in availability order in chunks of 512, each with a sender, a receiver, z from the compressor and the time since each host was last seen. After a chunk is scored, a message built from both memories, z and both time gaps (432 numbers) passes through a small network and a GRU into both hosts' memories. A host is read in two layers: its memory plus attention over up to 20 recent peers, then two learned global queries pooling over recently active hosts. The next-event head scores whether two hosts interact next; its error on the real event is the surprise. The ranking head compares each candidate host with both global queries and ranks the next target. Training uses the next-event loss, each real pair against one negative (its initiator with another event's responder from the same chunk), plus the ranking loss on attacker and victim roles, the true target against five negative candidates. A rollout imagines six events forward, the ranking head choosing each target. Calibration picks the served score on validation and sets its threshold at a 1-in-10,000 false-alarm budget.
